newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - AIDS prevention tough in developing world.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - AIDS prevention tough in developing world.

text.p: Zambian teenagers are afraid their sexual organs will shrivel up if they do not have sex.
Indonesian Moslems say promoting condom use will destroy public morals while many Thais think their government is lying to them about the dangers of AIDS.
The AIDS virus is hard enough to fight without having to deal with what is going on in people's heads, but health workers say prevention -- and education -- has to be the way ahead.
"Prevention is better than cure. Prevention is cheaper than cure," said Andrew Hobbs, a volunteer with the Anti-AIDS Project in Lusaka.

Powerful new combinations of drugs are making inroads against the HIV virus in the rich industrialised countries of Europe and North America. Condoms are accepted as indispensable and even drug users are turning to disposable syringes.

There is even some evidence that drug cocktails can stop transmission of the virus in bodily fluids such as sperm, and that giving drugs like AZT to new mothers can stop them from passing the virus to their babies.
But more than 90 percent of cases of HIV infection are in the developing world, where even an aspirin is a luxury and where entire villages have been wiped out by the deadly virus.
Health workers admit they may have to write off an older generation of Africans and concentrate on saving the young. They believe sex education is the only way forward.

"One-quarter of a generation of young parents has been wiped out," Hobbs said. "Even if me and my colleagues helped, even if no one in Zambia caught AIDS from tomorrow on, there would still be a huge problem for the next 30 years."
He added: "Drugs are in desperate short supply. Sometimes we don't even have aspirin."
Hobbs said his job was all the more difficult because he has to work with forbidden subject matter -- sexual behaviour.
"A lot of our work is actually trying to destroy myths and misconceptions," he said, speaking by telephone from Lusaka.

"Teenagers get a lot of their information from friends and half that information is wrong. A lot of these teenagers are living in fear because they think their sex organs will fall off if they do this or that."
For instance, girls tell one another that their vaginas will close up if they do not have sex. "Or they say if boys don't use their sperm it'll rot inside them."
Andy Jones of the British charity Voluntary Service Overseas, who taught at a high school in neighbouring Zimbabwe, said parents and teachers were often of little help.
"Although teachers are fully aware that there are kids at school having sex, they wouldn't dream of distributing condoms because that's seen as endorsing it," he said.
Similar problems persist in southeast Asia, especially in Moslem Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei and the mostly Roman Catholic Philippines.

Pressure from conservative Moslem clerics has stopped Indonesia's government from promoting the use of condoms, while the Catholic church in the Philippines is putting similar pressure on the government in Manila -- despite the obvious risks posed by the sex industry there.

A study by Thailand's Mahidol University found that although two-thirds of the population knew about HIV, 64 percent continued to indulge in high-risk behaviour such as sex with multiple partners and without the use of condoms.
People in the southern Thai provinces felt the government was exaggerating the dangers of AIDS, the survey found.

Such attitudes trouble the World Health Organisation, which predicts that by the year 2000 a million Thais, 750,000 Indonesians, 300,000 Vietnamese, 90,000 Filipinos and more than 20,000 Malaysians will be infected with HIV.
People will continue to have sex, no matter what. AIDS workers want to do give people the power to protect themselves within their own cultures, but this is not always easy.
Doris D'Cruz-Grote, a Berlin-based AIDS expert, said between 50 and 80 percent of all infected African women were in monogamous relationships.

"When a woman is economically powerless to negotiate her basic needs, or is subject to domestic violence and abuse, encouraging her to negotiate safer sex is unrealistic," she argued in an article for the Lancet medical journal.
Female sex workers often had no choice, she added.
Women could not demand that men use condoms, not least because men in many cultures want to have children, she said.
But giving women and children counselling could have advantages beyond giving them defences against AIDS, Hobbs said.
"Women have a lot less power and they have a lot less power in sexual relationships," he said. "This is being talked about for the first time because of AIDS."

Long-term, this could only be good, he added. "It has forced people to talk more about it, especially in a place like Zambia where people don't talk about sex openly. Men and women are questioning their relationships more."
The same goes for adolescents. Getting sex out from "behind the bike sheds" helps in other areas of their lives.
"We are trying to improve the self-image of teenagers -- prepare them for parenthood, help them feel better about their bodies," Hobbs said.
"We are also trying to give them positive attitudes -- negotiation skills, communication skills that would enable them to refuse to have sex."
Jones agreed. "It helps kids learn to value their lives. In that context, the fact that AIDS is the hook off which those issues are raised has to be a good thing."
